meta.title: Who originally recorded "My Way"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Frank Sinatra didn’t originate it. The record came first in November 1967 as “Comme d’habitude” by Claude François on Disques Flèche.
meta.ogDescription: Sinatra’s 1969 signature song is an English rewrite of a French single Claude François recorded in 1967 on his own label, Disques Flèche.

answer.label: Not a Frank Sinatra original — a 1967 Claude François single
answer.originalArtistDates: 1939-1978 · French pop singer, songwriter and label owner
answer.sourceLine: “My Way” is heard as Frank Sinatra’s own invention — the record he made to sum himself up. The song on it already existed: Claude François recorded it in Paris on 17 September 1967 as “Comme d’habitude” and released it that November on Disques Flèche, the label he owned. The music is by Jacques Revaux, with French lyrics by Gilles Thibaut and François himself ↗; Paul Anka bought the adaptation rights after hearing it on French radio and wrote an entirely new English lyric. The French original was a genuine hit at home — No. 3 on the French hit parade, more than 200,000 copies sold — but it is a song about a marriage gone quietly cold, not a life summed up without regret.

original.heading: Who recorded it first
original.label: Disques Flèche
original.released: Issued November 1967 in France as a 7-inch EP on Disques Flèche / Philips (catalogue 424 550 BE), alongside “L’Homme au traîneau” and “La plus belle chose du monde”. Recorded 17 September 1967 at Studio de la Gaîté, Paris, arranged by David Whitaker.
original.charted: A real French hit: No. 3 on the French hit parade by 3 February 1968, past 200,000 copies sold — but never an English-language record.
original.writer: Jacques Revaux (music); Claude François and Gilles Thibaut (original French lyrics); Paul Anka (English lyrics)
original.cover: Frank Sinatra recorded Paul Anka’s English adaptation on 30 December 1968 and Reprise released it in 1969. It peaked at No. 27 on the US Billboard Hot 100 and No. 5 in the UK, where it became famous for an extraordinarily long chart life.
trail: Composed by Jacques Revaux in February 1967 as an English-lyric demo called “For Me”, and turned down by a queue of French stars before Claude François took it and rewrote it with Gilles Thibaut — per the French-language account of the song ↗.
The November 1967 French EP is catalogued at MusicBrainz, with the Disques Flèche / Philips credit and catalogue number ↗.
Paul Anka acquired the adaptation and recording rights for a nominal one dollar, the original writers keeping their royalty shares — documented on the English song’s page ↗.

Before Anka’s lyric stuck, a young David Bowie was asked to attempt an English version; his “Even a Fool Learns to Love” was rejected and never commercially released — as recorded on the original song’s page ↗.

authors.name: Claude François
authors.heading: Made the record first
authors.bio: Born in Ismailia, Egypt, in 1939 and raised into French pop stardom, Claude François was one of France’s biggest sellers of the 1960s and 70s — a relentless showman who ran his own label, Flèche, and his own magazine. He cut “Comme d’habitude” in September 1967, sharing the lyric credit with Gilles Thibaut and the music credit with Jacques Revaux. He died in Paris in 1978, at 39, accidentally electrocuted in his bathroom.

authors.name: Frank Sinatra
authors.heading: Made the version the world knows
authors.bio: Sinatra recorded Paul Anka’s English lyric on 30 December 1968 and Reprise released it in 1969. The performance is the reason anyone outside France knows the tune at all: he sings it as a summing-up, unhurried and completely unembarrassed, and it followed him for the rest of his life. None of that is diminished by the chronology — the only error is thinking his record came first.

authors.name: Jacques Revaux, Gilles Thibaut & Paul Anka
authors.heading: Who actually wrote it
authors.metaLine: Music by Jacques Revaux; French lyrics by Gilles Thibaut and Claude François; English lyrics by Paul Anka
authors.bio: Jacques Revaux wrote the melody in February 1967, first shopping it around as an English-lyric demo called “For Me” that several French stars declined. Gilles Thibaut and Claude François gave it its French words, about a couple going through the motions of a marriage. Paul Anka, who had heard the record on French radio, bought the adaptation rights and wrote a completely different English lyric — the same tune carrying an entirely new subject.

misattribution.heading: Right song, wrong first record
misattribution.intro: The confusion here is not about who wrote it — it is about which record came first, and in which language.

items.why: His Reprise single is so completely identified with him that it reads as an original written to order. It is an English adaptation of an existing French record.
Recorded 17 September 1967 in Paris and released that November on Disques Flèche as “Comme d’habitude”. It reached No. 3 in France.

items.who: Jacques Revaux, Gilles Thibaut and Claude François — then Paul Anka
items.why: Revaux composed the music; Thibaut and François wrote the French lyric; Anka wrote the English one. Sinatra wrote none of it.

misattribution.truthLine: The first record of this melody is a French single from November 1967 — and its subject is a marriage gone cold, not a life without regrets.

context.heading: Why the cover swallowed the original
lead: Most eclipsed originals lose to a better arrangement. This one lost to a change of subject. “Comme d’habitude” is a small, domestic song — two people performing their marriage out of habit — and Claude François, whose own relationship was ending, sang it to a French audience that took it to No. 3. Paul Anka kept the melody and threw the meaning away, writing an English lyric about looking back over a whole life. That is a subject with no borders.

Then it went to the one singer who could make a summing-up sound earned rather than boastful. Sinatra’s record only reached No. 27 in the States, a useful reminder that the song did not conquer the world in a week — it seeped in, through weddings, retirements and funerals, until it was inescapable. By then the French single had been filed away as a curiosity, if it was known at all.
detailsBody: February 1967 — Jacques Revaux composes the melody and offers it around as “For Me”, with English words. Several French singers pass on it.
17 September 1967 — Claude François records it as “Comme d’habitude” at Studio de la Gaîté in Paris, with a new French lyric by Gilles Thibaut and himself, arranged by David Whitaker.
November 1967 — the record is released in France on Disques Flèche / Philips, catalogue 424 550 BE.
3 February 1968 — it stands at No. 3 on the French hit parade, on its way past 200,000 copies sold.
1968 — David Bowie is asked to write an English lyric; his attempt, “Even a Fool Learns to Love”, is rejected and never commercially released.
1968 — Paul Anka, having heard the song on French radio, acquires the adaptation rights for a nominal one dollar and writes a new English lyric aimed squarely at Sinatra.
30 December 1968 — Frank Sinatra records “My Way”. Reprise releases it in 1969; it peaks at No. 27 in the US and No. 5 in the UK.
context.pull: The tune crossed the Channel intact. The song did not.
